title: Netflix Moves Toward Open Source Flink Autoscaler for 30,000+ Streaming Jobs
gist: Netflix is migrating over 30,000 Apache Flink streaming jobs from a custom cluster-level autoscaler to the open-source Apache Flink Autoscaler (built on FLIP-271/DS2 research), with one team reporting a 58% cut in annualized Flink compute cost (~$1.1M/year) after moving to per-operator scaling decisions.

themes.theme: Why Netflix's original autoscaler hit a ceiling

insights.claim: Netflix's first Flink autoscaler, built around 2019 on Mantis and fed by Atlas cluster-level telemetry (CPU, network utilization, Kafka lag, input/consume rate), adjusted the total TaskManager count for a job and cut resource usage 25-45% across thousands of pipelines.
insights.speaker: Leela Kumili
insights.so_what: Establishes the cost baseline the new per-operator autoscaler is being measured against — a 25-45% historical savings floor that the new approach is now beating on specific pipelines.
insights.locator: Netflix has run Apache Flink since 2017 and built its first autoscaler around 2019

insights.claim: Because the original autoscaler reasoned at the cluster level, all operators in a job shared one scaling decision, which became a poor fit for stateful pipelines with branches, joins, and terabytes of state where different parts of the dataflow have different processing requirements.
insights.speaker: Leela Kumili
insights.so_what: Identifies the specific architectural limitation (cluster-level vs. operator-level granularity) that drove a costly re-platforming — a pattern other large stateful-streaming operators are likely to hit too.
insights.locator: The limitation was the scaling unit

themes.theme: How the OSS Flink Autoscaler works and its research lineage

insights.claim: The Apache Flink Autoscaler estimates each operator's true processing rate from throughput and busy-time metrics exposed by the running job, then walks the job graph to calculate required parallelism per vertex, as specified in FLIP-271 for heterogeneous streaming jobs.
insights.speaker: Leela Kumili
insights.so_what: Per-vertex, throughput-derived scaling is now a documented, community-standardized (FLIP-271) technique rather than a Netflix-proprietary trick, lowering the bar for other companies to adopt it.
insights.locator: The Apache Flink Autoscaler instead uses metrics exposed by the running job

insights.claim: The True Processing Rate technique underlying the autoscaler originated in the DS2 research project, which initially explored critical path analysis before adopting the simpler True Processing Rate baseline because it 'worked really well,' and this approach was subsequently folded into Flink's own autoscaling work.
insights.speaker: Vasiliki Kalavri
insights.so_what: A case where a simpler heuristic beat a more complex analytical method (critical path analysis) in production streaming systems — relevant precedent for evaluating academic-to-production tradeoffs in infra research generally.
insights.quote: It turned out that this very simple idea worked really well.
insights.locator: The technique also builds on research from the DS2 project

insights.claim: Netflix reports that one team reduced annualized Flink compute expenditure by 58%, saving approximately $1.1 million annually, after adopting the open-source per-operator autoscaler.
insights.speaker: Leela Kumili
insights.so_what: A concrete, auditable ROI figure ($1.1M/year on one team alone) that other Flink operators can use to benchmark expected savings from migrating to operator-level autoscaling.
insights.locator: Netflix reports that one team reduced annualized Flink compute expenditure by 58%

themes.theme: Netflix's integration engineering and operator-graph constraints

insights.claim: Netflix integrated the OSS autoscaler with its internal control plane rather than deploying it directly through the Flink Kubernetes Operator, using a Spring Boot service that relies on Temporal workflows to isolate autoscaling decisions per job.
insights.speaker: Leela Kumili
insights.so_what: Shows large-scale adopters of an OSS control loop often still need custom orchestration (Temporal-based isolation) around it — a services/integration cost investors should factor into 'open source adoption' cost estimates, not just licensing savings.
insights.locator: Netflix integrated the autoscaler with its internal control plane

insights.claim: To make the OSS autoscaler work at its scale, Netflix modified JobManager metric collection to support jobs with up to 3,000 subtasks, added server-side metric filtering, preserved forward-connected subgraphs during scaling, and added handling for sink backpressure.
insights.speaker: Leela Kumili
insights.so_what: Quantifies the scale ceiling (3,000 subtasks per job) the vanilla OSS component needed patching to reach — a data point for other operators assessing whether they'll hit the same wall.
insights.locator: Netflix also modified JobManager metric collection

insights.claim: Changing parallelism across a FORWARD connection in Flink can require redistribution; Netflix's implementation instead keeps forward-connected operators together during rescaling, addressing an issue that has also surfaced in Apache Flink developer discussions and is tracked separately as FLINK-38538 for busy operators affected by output-ratio-based scaling.
insights.speaker: Leela Kumili
insights.so_what: An open upstream issue (FLINK-38538) signals the autoscaler's scaling heuristics still have known edge cases — worth monitoring for anyone building production reliability on top of this component.
insights.locator: The forward connection issue has also appeared in Apache Flink developer discussions

themes.theme: Differentiation from generic autoscalers and forward roadmap

insights.claim: Unlike generic event-driven autoscalers such as KEDA, which scale workloads from external metrics or events, Flink's autoscaler reasons about the internal dataflow graph and per-operator capacity, making it purpose-built for stateful streaming rather than a general workload scaler.
insights.speaker: Leela Kumili
insights.so_what: Draws a clear product boundary between generic Kubernetes autoscalers (KEDA) and stream-graph-aware autoscalers — relevant for infra vendors positioning autoscaling products against each other.
insights.locator: Unlike generic event-driven autoscalers such as KEDA

insights.claim: Netflix currently runs the autoscaler at a 0.45 utilization target, well below Flink's 0.7 community default, specifically to reduce aggressive rescaling of large stateful jobs.
insights.speaker: Leela Kumili
insights.so_what: A concrete, non-default tuning parameter (0.45 vs 0.7) that reveals Netflix trades some compute efficiency for rescaling stability — a tunable other large stateful-job operators should evaluate rather than assume the community default is optimal.
insights.locator: Netflix currently uses a 0.45 utilization target

insights.claim: Netflix plans to migrate its remaining internal autoscaling use cases to the open-source Flink Autoscaler implementation, while investigating Flink 2's disaggregated state architecture as a way to address the cost of state recovery during rescaling.
insights.speaker: Leela Kumili
insights.so_what: Signals continued full consolidation onto OSS tooling and flags disaggregated state (Flink 2) as the next cost lever to watch for further stateful-streaming cost reductions industry-wide.
insights.locator: The company plans to migrate its remaining internal autoscaling use cases
